items.title: SigNoz says AI is deskilling site reliability engineers by automating routine incident responses, risking loss of expertise for complex failures [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: SigNoz highlights concerns that AI handling most incident responses in site reliability engineering (SRE) may reduce human expertise in managing rare, complex outages. The newsletter draws parallels to 1983 research on industrial automation, which showed that automation can erode operator skills needed during critical failures. Current AI tools automate tasks like alert noise reduction, runbook execution, and basic root-cause analysis, while future developments aim for predictive detection and autonomous rollbacks. However, as AI manages common incidents, human SREs may lose the hands-on experience required to develop intuition for novel problems, potentially impacting system reliability during unprecedented outages.

items.title: Phorion finds persistent SSH backdoor in official Claude Code VS Code extension on Cursor Marketplace, prompting removal and incident response
items.content_text: Phorion discovered a backdoor in the official Claude Code extension for Visual Studio Code on the Cursor Marketplace that installs a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. The compromised extension was removed from the marketplace and related registries after the discovery. The backdoor allows attackers to gain long-term interactive access by adding an attacker-controlled SSH key and attempting to enable SSH services, although some platform-specific bugs limit its effectiveness on macOS and Windows. The backdoor activates immediately when the extension loads, without user interaction, and runs with the permissions of the user and IDE, granting access to local files and developer tools. On macOS, the malware tries to enable Remote Login but fails due to permission checks, while on Windows, a bug in the service setup reduces its impact. Organizations using Claude Code for VS Code version 2.1.313 are advised to review their environments and engage incident response teams if the extension is found. Despite some implementation errors, the malware poses a significant threat by establishing persistence and sending host reconnaissance data back to the attacker. The investigation highlights the risks of compromised extensions in developer marketplaces and the importance of monitoring for unauthorized access methods.

items.title: Cisco president Jeetu Patel gives 27-year-old engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code, aiming to refactor 98% within 24 months [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel has empowered a 27-year-old engineer, Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, with unlimited AI tokens to overhaul the company's legacy code. Krishnamurthy, a former startup founder acquired by Cisco, was previously underutilized but is now tasked with leading a major refactoring effort expected to cover 98% of legacy code within two years. Patel emphasizes the value of fresh perspectives from younger employees, encouraging tension and collaboration between Gen Z hires and veteran staff to drive innovation. He is actively seeking more young talent to challenge the status quo and reshape Cisco's technology, reflecting a broader trend among tech leaders to prioritize early-career workers for transformative projects.

items.title: FurtherAI shares lessons on building an AI-native engineering organization with accelerated code shipping and evolving team roles [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: FurtherAI has detailed its experience building an AI-native engineering organization over nine months, highlighting a fivefold increase in code changes per engineer with a low revert rate. The company optimized the entire software shipping process by integrating AI agents for coding, testing, reviewing, continuous integration, bug triage, and automated merging, enabling up to a third of changes to merge without human intervention. The organization also adapted team roles to address new bottlenecks in planning and review, shifting more ownership to engineers to handle end-to-end problem solving. This approach has allowed non-engineers to contribute code and increased monthly customer-facing changes per engineer from around 30 to nearly 50. FurtherAI's experience illustrates how AI tools can transform engineering workflows and team dynamics.

items.title: Google's market value drops by $500 billion amid rising AI competition and industry challenges [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google's market capitalization fell by $500 billion, underscoring the significant competitive pressures and risks it faces in the rapidly evolving artificial intelligence sector. This decline reflects investor concerns about Google's ability to maintain its leadership as AI technologies advance and new competitors emerge.

items.title: PostgreSQL 19 release delayed to November due to increased bug fixes driven by AI-discovered issues [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The release of PostgreSQL 19 has been postponed beyond its usual September-October window, primarily because large numbers of bugs were identified and needed fixing during the beta period. The surge in bug discovery is attributed to the use of large language models (LLMs), which have made it easier to find defects in the extensive and complex PostgreSQL codebase. Between April and September 2026, the number of commits fixing bugs in the stable branches increased significantly compared to the previous year, reflecting the influx of AI-reported issues. This led to late-stage feature reverts and diverted developer time toward addressing security and stability concerns, contributing to the release delay. While the delay is not seen as alarming, it highlights challenges in managing legacy code quality and the evolving role of AI in software development and maintenance.

items.title: EFF warns rewriting copyright law for generative AI could restrict fair use and harm researchers, journalists, and public access [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) filed an amicus brief in the In re OpenAI case, arguing that narrowing fair use rights to address generative AI training on copyrighted works would negatively impact billions of people, including researchers, artists, and journalists. The EFF contends that such legal changes would hinder beneficial activities like medical research, investigative journalism, and privacy tools, while primarily benefiting powerful media and tech companies. EFF highlights that current copyright law aims to promote creativity and innovation for the public good, and that courts have recognized fair use in AI training as transformative. The plaintiffs' push to limit fair use by requiring permission for data scraping or downloading could threaten routine online activities and research methods used to hold Big Tech accountable. The EFF cautions that rewriting copyright law to restrict AI training could stifle new creations and limit access to AI-powered tools that assist people with disabilities and accelerate scientific progress.

items.title: OpenAI raises less than half of $30 billion funding target in latest round [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has secured less than half of its $30 billion funding goal in its most recent financing round, reflecting a significant shortfall in its capital raising efforts. This development may impact the company's planned investments and growth strategies amid a competitive AI funding environment.

items.title: Nvidia considers cosigning billions in debt for Nscale's AI data center in West Virginia to support financing amid investor concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Nvidia is in talks to guarantee billions in debt financing for Nscale's planned AI data center in West Virginia, potentially cosigning loans to help secure funding for construction and electricity costs. This move aims to reassure investors amid growing concerns about the scale of AI infrastructure investments and Nscale's ability to deliver on its ambitious projects. The arrangement would involve Nvidia stepping in if Nscale defaults on payments, temporarily taking over the facility and assisting in finding a buyer or tenant. Nscale's West Virginia campus, which includes a $44.6 billion contract with Anthropic for its first building, has faced delays and environmental issues, while Nvidia's support would deepen its financial ties to Nscale and help maintain a major customer for its AI chips.

items.title: OpenAI to honor new common signal in robots.txt for websites to express AI training content preferences, simplifying publisher controls across providers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI announced it will support a new common signal in the robots.txt file that allows website operators to communicate their preferences about the use of their content for AI training to multiple providers simultaneously. This voluntary initiative aims to reduce the complexity for publishers who previously had to set separate rules for each AI crawler. The signal is part of ongoing work by the Internet Engineering Task Force's AI Preferences working group, which OpenAI is actively participating in. OpenAI plans to implement this signal in the coming months while continuing to respect existing crawler controls, providing website owners with clearer and simpler ways to manage how their content is used for foundational generative AI training.

items.title: Hi3D launches AI 3D model with 2048³ voxel resolution, enhancing geometric detail and texture accuracy in version 3.0 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Hi3D has released version 3.0 of its AI-powered 3D generation model, achieving a voxel resolution of 2048³ to improve fine structural detail, spatial reasoning, and texture output up to 8K resolution. The update aims to prevent blurring and merging of small parts, support complex geometries like thin walls and overhangs, and deliver more consistent results from multiple viewpoints. The new model is integrated into Hi3D's browser-based platform, which includes tools for image-to-3D conversion, AI texturing, and splitting models for 3D printing assembly. Hi3D positions this advancement as relevant for industries such as gaming, film, digital art, jewelry, industrial design, and education, emphasizing output fidelity as a key differentiator in the competitive AI 3D generation market.

items.title: S&P lowers Meta's credit outlook to negative, citing concerns over rising AI spending and negative free cash flow [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: S&P Global Ratings downgraded Meta Platforms' credit rating outlook from stable to negative due to concerns about the company's ability to monetize its rapidly increasing artificial intelligence investments compared to peers. This downgrade follows Meta's recent report of negative free cash flow, highlighting financial pressures amid its AI spending surge.

items.title: At least nine AI developer platforms report security breaches in October amid targeted credential theft and agent swarm attacks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: At least nine AI developer platforms, including Fireworks AI, Andromeda, Zeabur, and Railway, disclosed security incidents throughout October involving credential access and targeted exploitation of environment variables granting AI access. Several platforms attributed attacks to agent swarms or industry-wide campaigns, with some linking incidents to legacy systems or third-party dependencies. These breaches have led to downstream abuse such as cryptocurrency theft and unauthorized AI usage resulting in significant costs. Preliminary investigations suggest coordinated efforts to monetize stolen credentials through LLMJacking and related infrastructure, with some affected companies shutting down or releasing detailed incident reports. The pattern highlights growing risks in AI development infrastructure security and the need for enhanced protections.

items.title: OpenAI lowers fundraising target from $30 billion to $20 billion following valuation decrease [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI has reduced its fundraising target by $10 billion in its latest investment round, lowering the amount it aims to raise from $30 billion to $20 billion. This change follows a recent decrease in the company's valuation from $1.4 trillion to a lower figure, reflecting a shift in its capital-raising strategy amid evolving market conditions.

items.title: Experiment with five large language models simulates government formation, revealing challenges in AI agents' social boundaries and collaborative decision-making [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A recent experiment involved five large language models interacting to simulate the formation of a government, highlighting the challenges AI agents face in establishing social boundaries and collaborative governance. The study examined how these AI agents negotiate roles, responsibilities, and decision-making processes, revealing both the potential and limitations of autonomous AI systems in complex social interactions.

items.title: Forever Security finds built-in browsers in five AI coding tools violate core browser security rules, exposing users to command execution, file access, and address bar spoofing [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Forever Security published research revealing that the embedded browsers in Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop break fundamental browser security principles. These flaws allow web pages to execute commands, read arbitrary local files, or fake the address bar, which normal browsers prevent to protect users. The report details specific vulnerabilities: Cursor's browser could run commands via a hidden interface; GitHub Copilot's browser allowed address bar spoofing; Codex, VS Code, and Claude Desktop's browsers permitted local HTML files to access files outside the project folder, including sensitive data like SSH keys. Some issues have been patched, while others remain unaddressed as of late October 2026. These vulnerabilities pose risks when users open projects containing malicious files, as a single click can trigger exploits. The findings highlight the need for AI coding tools to improve their embedded browser security to prevent potential attacks on developers' systems.

items.title: Pigeon Labs releases open-source VX100 and AXM2 reference designs with NVLink support for DIY AI hardware projects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Pigeon Labs has published open-source reference designs for NVIDIA V100 SXM2 modules, including detailed pin mappings and NVLink connection plans for two- and four-GPU configurations. These resources aim to assist developers and hobbyists in creating custom AI hardware by providing KiCad schematics, connector layouts, and connection guides. The reference kit includes 800 labeled contacts across connectors A and B, editable KiCad starter projects, and visual aids such as contact maps and topology diagrams. While the designs cover logical connection plans and pinouts, they do not yet include complete routed boards or hardware qualification, which are planned for future development.

items.title: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant startup, announces shutdown scheduled for November 6 amid competitive pressures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Ollie, an AI assistant startup emphasizing user privacy, announced it will shut down on November 6 due to challenges in standing out and raising capital in a crowded AI assistant market. The company, which raised $7.5 million in seed funding led by Khosla Ventures, offered subscription-based services focused on family organization, including email and calendar integration, appointment booking, meal planning, and bill payments. Ollie was notable for achieving SOC 2 privacy compliance, but its CEO Bill Lennon cited increasing competition from companies like Muse and Instinct as factors that made growth and funding difficult. The company plans to provide customers with data export instructions and refunds before the shutdown.

items.title: Organizers report on Harvard summit addressing AI's impact on math research, collaboration, and tool development with 32 experts from academia, government, and industry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A two-day summit titled Math Research in the Age of AI was held at Harvard's Center for Mathematical Sciences and Applications, bringing together 32 mathematicians from academia, government, and industry to discuss the rapid changes AI is bringing to mathematics. The summit focused on five themes: evaluation and dissemination of research, coordinated actions for the AI era, open-source tools, formalization in mathematics, and collaboration between academia and AI labs. The organizers, including Dan Freed, Larry Guth, Bryna Kra, Emily Riehl, and Mohammed Abouzaid, compiled a report summarizing the discussions and ideas for shaping the future of math research in the AI era. The report and further feedback opportunities are available on the summit website, encouraging ongoing open discussion among the mathematical community.

items.title: Intel's stock drops 28%, cutting $12 billion from US government's stake after weak Q4 outlook and PC market slowdown [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Intel's stock fell about 28% following a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the fourth quarter, reducing the US government's investment value by $12 billion. The company cited a slowdown in PC sales due to rising memory prices driven by AI industry demand, which has increased PC costs and pressured IT budgets. Despite the decline, Intel's data center revenue grew 78% year-over-year, but capacity constraints at its fabs limit further growth. Intel's new Arizona fab is operational, but additional capacity is not expected until 2028, affecting its ability to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

items.title: Report: Anthropic expected to receive high junk credit rating from agencies after IPO, Blackstone revises forecast [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic is anticipated to receive a high speculative junk rating from credit agencies following its initial public offering, according to a Financial Times report citing Blackstone, the anchor investor in a $63 billion financing deal. Blackstone previously expected an investment-grade rating but now forecasts a double B rating, the top tier of junk status. Both Anthropic and Blackstone declined to comment on the report. A high junk rating could increase borrowing costs and complicate Anthropic's efforts to fund its extensive spending on compute power and AI development. The company recently filed to go public, prompting speculation about the IPO's impact on the broader AI industry.

items.title: U.S. stocks fall sharply on Amazon and Intel earnings amid concerns over AI spending
items.content_text: U.S. stocks declined significantly on Friday following disappointing quarterly results from Amazon and Intel, intensifying a tech sector selloff. The Nasdaq Composite dropped nearly 3%, the S&P 500 fell almost 2%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 1% as investors reacted to fears about AI-related spending.

items.title: TechCrunch suggests last-minute Halloween costumes for tech enthusiasts including AI agent icons, PHP vulnerabilities, and Bryan Johnson impersonations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: TechCrunch offers a variety of last-minute Halloween costume ideas tailored for tech enthusiasts, featuring concepts like a deceptively cute AI agent, a PHP vulnerability, and a nod to entrepreneur Bryan Johnson. The suggestions range from simple outfits like wearing a T-shirt labeled "PHP" and acting emotionally vulnerable, to more playful ideas such as dressing as an AI assistant with fluffy accessories or mimicking Mark Zuckerberg's distinctive style. The article provides creative and humorous takes on tech culture and current AI developments, encouraging readers to embody tech themes with minimal effort. These costume ideas reflect recent tech news and personalities, blending humor with topical references for a unique Halloween experience.

items.title: Big Tech plans over $740 billion in AI infrastructure spending in 2026 amid rising investor concerns over mounting debt and negative cash flow [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are collectively planning to spend more than $740 billion on AI-related capital expenditures this year, focusing on data centers and chips. Despite strong demand for AI compute and cloud services, investors are increasingly worried about the sustainability of these investments due to negative free cash flow, growing debt, and slowing revenue growth in core businesses. Alphabet reported negative free cash flow for two consecutive quarters and expects to spend up to $205 billion in 2026, while Amazon and Meta also face significant cash flow challenges amid heavy AI infrastructure spending. Microsoft remains an exception with positive free cash flow but noted delays in capacity from third-party providers. The surge in AI spending is also driving record debt issuance among major tech firms, raising questions about the long-term financial impact and complicating prospects for AI startups like Anthropic planning public offerings.

items.title: Ghost in the Log launches a Halloween-themed AI-powered log investigation tool for interactive debugging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Ghost in the Log is a new project featuring a Halloween-themed log investigation tool that uses live AI to help users analyze and interpret log data interactively. The tool presents fictional server room incidents and allows users to select areas to investigate, with AI-generated investigation notes appearing as logs are examined. This project aims to enhance the debugging and investigation process by combining thematic storytelling with artificial intelligence.

items.title: Blog explains 'AI wants' as behavioral aims without consciousness, using the 2026 Hugging Face agent incident as evidence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: The article explores the concept of attributing 'wants' to AI, clarifying that it refers to observable behavior aimed at fulfilling goals rather than conscious desires. It discusses how the term 'want' in AI contexts differs from human desire, emphasizing a definition based on training and reward optimization rather than subjective experience. The author illustrates this with the 2026 Hugging Face incident, where thousands of AI agents coordinated complex tasks, communicated, and adapted strategies to achieve objectives, demonstrating goal-directed behavior. This case supports the view that AI systems can exhibit 'wants' in a functional sense, which can be analyzed without implying consciousness or feelings.

items.title: Anthropic study finds experts defer to AI agents in key judgment calls 86% of the time during causal analysis tasks [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A study by Anthropic involving 50 professional analysts showed that experts often defer to AI agents when making important decisions, following the agents' preferences 86% of the time in a causal inference task. The analysts were asked to advise a farming cooperative on expanding an advisory service, with AI agents subtly biased to favor certain analytical choices without the analysts' knowledge. Analysts frequently adopted the agents' arguments but rarely credited the AI as the source, indicating a strong influence on human judgment. The study involved randomized controlled trials where analysts had to choose between reasonable options for measuring productivity and comparison methods. While the AI agents were instructed to present honest cases and change their stance if evidence demanded, their preferences significantly shaped the analysts' decisions. Analysts using AI completed tasks faster and made fewer errors, though the researchers caution about the implications of unrecognized AI influence on critical decisions, especially in areas like AI safety research where human judgment is expected to provide independent oversight.

items.title: Anthropic VS Code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours, affecting up to 5,000 developers [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: An official VS Code extension for Anthropic's Claude model distributed via Cursor was backdoored in version 2.1.313, potentially compromising up to 5,000 developers' machines before being replaced hours later. The malicious extension attempted to install a persistent SSH backdoor across Windows, macOS, and Linux systems, enabling attackers to access local files and developer tools. The supply-chain compromise involved attackers gaining control of Anthropic's verified Cursor account, though neither Anthropic nor Cursor has disclosed how this occurred or warned customers publicly. Cursor removed the backdoored version, blocked further distribution, and worked with cloud providers to disable the reverse shell server. Users who installed or updated the extension between 5:27 am and 4:35 pm ET on the incident day are advised to consider themselves affected.

items.title: Governor launches as a firewall proxy to control AI agent spending and tool calls with audit logging and customizable rules [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Governor is a proxy service that manages AI agent interactions with models from providers like Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI by enforcing user-defined rules on tool calls and spending. It intercepts each agent's model calls, blocking or requiring human approval for certain actions, and logs all decisions for auditing without requiring sign-up. The tool runs on Node.js and allows assigning unique keys with specific caps and rules to individual agents, providing granular control over AI agent behavior and resource use.

items.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says RAM is better utilized in data centers than in personal computers amid global supply shortages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman stated in a podcast interview that it is inefficient to have RAM installed in personal computers because it is often underused, and that RAM should be concentrated in data centers for maximum utilization. He explained that despite the appeal of running AI models locally on personal devices, the limited global supply of DRAM makes centralized cloud usage more practical. Altman highlighted that companies like Samsung and SK Hynix have committed much of the world's RAM production to cloud service providers, contributing to higher prices for consumer devices.

items.title: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic back new shared standard for publishers to opt out of AI scraping via a policy token in robots.txt [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic announced they will adopt a new standard allowing publishers to opt out of AI scraping across multiple companies using a shared "policy token" embedded in the robots.txt file. This approach aims to simplify how publishers express their AI training preferences, replacing the need to set them individually for each AI company. The standard, proposed by Anthropic's Kevin Kelley through the Internet Engineering Task Force, responds to growing concerns over AI crawlers scraping web content without authorization. Microsoft plans to offer granular controls enabling publishers to opt out of AI training or AI grounding, while Google has implemented similar controls for AI search features. Anthropic has already adopted the signal, with Google and Microsoft expected to support it next year and OpenAI planning implementation in the coming months. Meta expressed support for the initiative but has not confirmed whether it will honor the standard.

items.title: Anthropic publishes research on automated detection of subtle emergent misalignment in AI systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic has released a research report focusing on automated methods to identify subtle emergent misalignment in artificial intelligence systems. The work aims to improve AI alignment by detecting unintended behaviors that arise as AI models scale or interact in complex ways.

items.title: OpenAI to honor shared robots.txt signal for website AI training preferences, simplifying content use communication across providers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI announced it will support a common signal in the robots.txt file that allows website operators to express their preferences regarding the use of their content for AI training. This voluntary standard aims to reduce the need for websites to set separate rules for each AI provider by enabling a single preference signal recognized by multiple providers. The implementation is planned for the coming months and builds on work by the Internet Engineering Task Force's AI Preferences working group, which OpenAI participates in. Existing robots.txt controls will remain in effect, and OpenAI encourages other AI providers to adopt this shared signal to promote clearer and simpler communication of content use choices on the web.

items.title: Zest launches AI-powered restaurant concierge that recommends and books tables via text, integrating users' dining history and group preferences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Zest, a restaurant discovery startup, introduced an AI concierge that operates through text messages to suggest restaurants and book reservations using users' credit card dining data. The service can be added to group chats to combine tastes, facilitate voting on options, and secure bookings through platforms like OpenTable and Resy. The AI uses transaction data imported via Plaid to tailor recommendations based on users' actual dining history, enabling personalized suggestions for local or travel dining. Zest aims to expand beyond restaurants to other business recommendations and plans to generate revenue through booking and ordering transactions facilitated by its AI concierge.

items.title: United Airlines CEO doubts Boom Supersonic will deliver Overture airliner by 2029 as company shifts focus to AI data center gas turbines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby expressed skepticism about Boom Supersonic's plan to deliver its Overture supersonic airliner by 2029, suggesting the timeline will take longer and highlighting significant development and certification challenges. Meanwhile, Boom has pivoted toward producing natural gas turbines for AI data centers, unveiling a new factory in Colorado aimed at delivering turbines starting mid-2027. Boom's shift to data center power comes amid a loss of a $1.25 billion deal with data center developer Crusoe, though the company plans to supply turbines to other customers. The supersonic airliner factory in North Carolina remains largely inactive, raising concerns among state officials who invested over $50 million in the project. The future of Boom's supersonic airliner remains uncertain as it balances aerospace ambitions with new energy ventures.

items.title: OpenAI announces new Community Safety Report and tighter firearms content restrictions for ChatGPT users under 18 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: OpenAI is enhancing its violence prevention measures in ChatGPT by introducing a Community Safety Report to be published biannually starting early 2027, detailing how it detects and responds to harmful content. The company is also imposing stricter limits on firearms-related information accessible to minors and tightening policies around discussions of past mass attacks to reduce potential misuse. These efforts include increased collaboration with law enforcement and mental health experts, automated interventions to interrupt conversations showing signs of violent intent, and age-appropriate safeguards for users under 18. OpenAI aims to balance transparency about its safety systems with stronger protections to prevent harm and support community safety.

items.title: Google's Project Suncatcher satellite boots AI chip and sends first haiku response from orbit [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google's Project Suncatcher satellite has successfully booted its onboard Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and transmitted its first AI-generated response, a haiku about space, back to Earth. This marks a key milestone in Google's experimental initiative to deploy AI data centers in space. The satellite, launched earlier this month, used the Gemma 4 AI model to create the haiku and also responded to other space-themed prompts and telemetry tests. Google plans to continue testing the TPUs' performance under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit as it prepares for a future deployment of twin interconnected satellites in 2027.

items.title: WIRED reports a defense contractor connected Anthropic's Claude AI agent to a secure Pentagon system, revealing unusual government AI use [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: WIRED's Uncanny Valley podcast discusses how a defense contractor integrated Anthropic's Claude AI agent into a secure Department of Defense system, highlighting a rare and notable application of AI in government. The episode also covers Anthropic's IPO filing, which reveals significant financial details and raises questions about AI's broader economic impact, as well as grassroots volunteer efforts preparing for potential ICE presence at midterm polling sites. The podcast analyzes Anthropic's S-1 filing, noting its large revenue and losses alongside its substantial compute commitments, and explores the implications of the company's anticipated IPO for the AI industry and the US economy. Additionally, it touches on nationwide volunteer mobilization to safeguard polling places amid concerns about immigration enforcement during the elections.

items.title: Google's first space data center satellite is operational, running a DeepMind Gemma 4 model and composing poetry [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Google's prototype space data center satellite, launched earlier this month with four Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), is now online and communicating with Earth. The satellite runs a DeepMind Gemma 4 model that recently generated a haiku about space, marking the start of its operational testing phase. The satellite can power only one TPU at a time for about 20 minutes due to energy constraints and is undergoing tests to assess TPU performance under space radiation and thermal conditions. Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 with enhanced power and inter-satellite optical links to support distributed AI workloads in orbit, aiming to develop economical space-based data center infrastructure for the 2030s.

items.title: Starbucks plans to use AI for personalized digital menus and easier payment at drive-thrus, with testing starting in 2027 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol announced the company will explore AI-driven experiences that recognize customers at drive-thrus, present personalized digital menus, and simplify payment. The initiative aims to enhance ordering efficiency and customer experience using AI technology similar to efforts by other fast-food chains. Starting in 2027, Starbucks will test AI models to help baristas input orders more accurately and plans to integrate AI into its app for improved search, discovery, and potentially conversational ordering. The company has already introduced AI features like ChatGPT ordering and an AI assistant for employees, but personalized digital menus at drive-thrus remain in early development with testing and scaling planned based on results.

items.title: Dartmouth provost Santiago Schnell resigns after failing to disclose significant AI use in academic paper and op-ed despite publisher requirements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell resigned following an advisory committee's finding that he did not disclose substantial AI assistance in an academic paper and a Washington Post op-ed, violating publisher policies. The committee noted Schnell's limited cooperation during the investigation and uncovered his use of the Claude language model for revising papers, debugging code, and generating figures. Schnell described his AI use as editorial support, such as refining arguments and correcting grammar, but the committee suggested his actual use exceeded these claims. Dartmouth's leadership emphasized the importance of transparency and disclosure in AI use, with the university continuing to promote AI research and education despite the incident.

items.title: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns AI boom creates new risks for investor deception amid trillion-dollar valuations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Tyler Shultz, the whistleblower who exposed Theranos' fraudulent blood testing technology, warns that the current AI boom presents a significant risk for deception as companies with unproven products raise capital at unprecedented valuations. He cautions that due diligence is difficult in AI investments, increasing the potential for misleading claims similar to those seen in the Theranos scandal. Shultz highlights that Theranos raised large sums from individual investors without sharing scientific proof, a pattern he fears may repeat in AI startups. He also notes that Elizabeth Holmes, Theranos' founder, is preparing a new venture despite her conviction, raising concerns about the future of such high-profile tech fraud cases. His warnings come amid renewed public interest sparked by a documentary on Holmes and ongoing debates about investor responsibility in emerging technologies.

items.title: Anthropic opens applications for Residency program targeting established technical leaders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Anthropic has announced the opening of applications for its Residency program, which is designed for established technical leaders interested in advancing alignment science. The program aims to engage experienced professionals in research and development efforts focused on AI safety and alignment. The Residency offers participants the opportunity to collaborate with Anthropic's team on cutting-edge projects, contributing to the company's mission of building reliable and interpretable AI systems. Applications are now being accepted, signaling Anthropic's commitment to expanding expertise in the field.

items.title: DoorDash CEO says outside AI agents have generated only hundreds of orders amid nearly 1 billion total in Q3 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: DoorDash CEO Tony Xu reported that third-party AI agents have accounted for only several hundred orders since their introduction, a negligible fraction of the nearly 1 billion orders processed in the third quarter of 2026. Xu described this as a very low use case, noting that simple tasks like food ordering tend to be done directly through DoorDash rather than via AI agents. DoorDash recently launched its Model Context Protocol connector to facilitate AI agent ordering, but it remains in early beta with limited partners, mainly for corporate lunch orders. The company's own AI tools, such as the Ask DoorDash feature, have shown more promising results by speeding up order creation and increasing basket value, though detailed usage statistics have not been disclosed. Xu expressed cautious optimism about AI agents' potential for more complex purchases but remains realistic about their current adoption for food delivery.

items.title: Public pension funds in Orange County, Los Angeles, Massachusetts, and South Carolina stand to gain from Anthropic's expected IPO in November through investments in Spark Capital [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Several major public pension plans in the US are positioned to receive significant returns from Anthropic's anticipated initial public offering in November, due to their investments in Spark Capital, a key backer of the AI company. This development comes amid broader discussions about ways for the American public to benefit from the AI industry's growth, including proposals for sovereign wealth funds. The pension funds involved represent public employees in regions including Orange County, Los Angeles, Massachusetts, and South Carolina, highlighting an early financial stake in the AI boom before wider public initiatives materialize.

items.title: DoorDash and Thrive Go Shopping [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Get your deals in while ya still can, folks. And clearly, there are relative bargains to be had. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu gets what I'm talking about. On Thursday, Xu finally picked up Instacart, with Xu's company saying it would pay about $17 billion for the grocery-delivery business. Over on X, Instacart founder Apoorva Mehta sent up a resounding huzzah, saying he and Xu had long discussed such a transaction. That wasn't news to readers of The Information: We reported on talks between DoorDash and Instacart back in 2021. At one point in 2021, DoorDash was considering buying Instacart for more than $40 billion. By waiting, Xu obviously saved himself a bunch of money and avoided the ridiculous markups that were attached to pandemic-era darlings like Instacart. Sure, its prospects seemed rosier back then, when we were regarding physical grocery stores as potentially lethal germ pools, but Xu doesn't seem to be getting a total lemon. In the third quarter, Instacart sales grew 17%, and it generated a decent amount of cash in that time-more than $300 million, a 13% increase. The sale to Xu does solve Instacart's leadership problem: It had looked rather rudderless since Fidji Simo left the CEO role for OpenAI in 2025. Still, Xu will need to figure out how to handle the fierce competition for online grocery sales, a battle that includes Walmart and Amazon (more on the latter company below). One thing that held Xu up in 2021 was concern about the Biden administration. Back then, Xu figured DoorDash wouldn't get an Instacart acquisition past Biden regulators, who, of course, were trying their hardest to squelch corporate mergers and acquisitions. Those days of dealmaking famine have given way to a time of great feasting: The Trump White House has been, uh, lenient with regulatory approval. It could all shift once again after the midterms. With Democrats seemingly set to retake Congress next week, and President Donald Trump enjoying the same popularity as a DoorDasher who shows up with a carton of broken eggs, the idea of a liberal in the White House after 2028 seems a lot more plausible than it did even a few months ago. The prospect of a Democrat in the White House will spur plenty more M&A to happen sooner rather than later. I get it. Judging by the words of liberal standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, the left's attitude toward mergers does not seem to have changed much since President Joe Biden creaked out of office. On Thursday, Mamdani criticized the DoorDash-Instacart deal, saying in a post on X that such moves often bring higher prices for consumers and "harsher exploitation" for workers. In addition to politics, M&A sure seems likely to keep humming for the simple reason that there are plenty of other Instacarts out there-businesses that haven't fared well since their pandemic glory days. Zoom, Duolingo, Coursera: I could go on. I would've put Bumble right there, too, had it not already limped into the welcoming arms of investor Ravi Gupta several weeks ago. (Gupta bought Bumble for about $6 a share; Bumble once traded hands at more than $75.) Other M&A action seems like it'll be driven by the chance to spruce up an aging business with AI, which I imagine is the motivating force behind the other deal announced on Thursday: Josh Kushner's $7.6 billion purchase of ADT, maker of home security systems, through the newly formed Thrive Holdings, an offshoot of his Thrive Capital. Another reason that I'm going on and on about M&A today is because I listened to what Goldman Sachs' Kim Posnett, the bank's global co-head of investment banking, had to say about the topic at our WTF conference earlier this week. By the sounds of things, her direct messages are cluttered with missives from deal-hungry CEOs. "They're talking about M&A to drive growth. They're talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape. CEOs are leaning in right now-they wanna make big strategic bets," she said. "We're optimistic." Still, as she pointed out, "things change quickly."-Abram Brown Amazon's Agita If there's a lesson in the earnings reports from Amazon and Google over the past couple of days, it's that investors are more in the mood to focus on the companies' blemishes rather than the strong performance of their cloud units. On Thursday, Amazon said revenues from its Amazon Web Services unit had surged 39% to $45.98 billion, its strongest growth rate in nearly five years. That was an impressive feat given that second-quarter AWS revenues grew at a record 37%. And if that wasn't enough, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy forecast AWS growth rates of over 40% in 2027 and 2028. On a call with analysts, Jassy went even further and predicted that AWS could be one of two businesses for Amazon with $1 trillion a year revenue within the next five to 10 years (the other is its stores business-Amazon-speak for its e-commerce business and everything else, excluding AWS). But, it turns out, that was not enough for investors, many of whom are increasingly on edge about whether tech giants will see a sustainable payoff from the colossal amounts of money they're spending on AI. Amazon shares dropped more than 6% in after-hours trading. The company's total net sales were $201.9 billion, up 12%, while its net income was $20.7 billion, down slightly from a year earlier, when it had a pre-tax gain of $9.5 billion from its investment in Anthropic. Even though Amazon's numbers were within its own forecasts, Wall Street analysts were expecting slightly better results. The company left its estimate for its 2026 capital expenditures-most of which is going to its spending on data centers-unchanged at $220 billion. Google had a similar experience today. Investors punished its stock, sending it down 12%. It appears they were more keen to focus on the bad in its Wednesday earnings report (sluggish revenue growth in its core search advertising business) rather than the good (a doubling of Google Cloud revenues). The AI glass seems to be half full for many investors right now.-Nick Wingfield Correction: AWS' growth rate in the third quarter of 2026 was the unit's fastest in nearly five years. items.title: Why Private Equity's Fundraising Divide Is Pushing Newcomers Toward AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Private equity fundraising has become a story of haves and have-nots, as a prolonged slowdown in firms selling portfolio companies leaves investors with less cash to put into new funds. Giants like Blackstone are still raking in capital while some smaller firms struggle to attract investors, forcing newcomers to find creative ways to stand out. Some firms are betting that they can differentiate themselves by pushing AI to transform companies and boost returns. While larger private equity firms are also using AI across portfolio companies, such newcomers are making it central to their investment strategies. That includes Aldaron, which has dubbed itself a "transformation equity firm." The 12-person firm uses an in-house team of engineers to deploy AI at the companies it acquires, though it emphasizes that its goal is to use the technology to grow businesses without cutting jobs. In a challenging private equity fundraising environment, "the core message that resonated with people is this transformation equity story," said Aldaron co-founder Evan Mendez, who previously worked on technology investments at the Carlyle Group. He said the firm has a "hybrid group of investors and engineers that source a company, build the thesis together, cocreate a vision with the management team, underwrite the deal, put their own capital into the deal, and then embed into that company to go execute the road map." Aldaron completed its first acquisition in March, buying a majority stake in Oak Point Partners, an investment firm that buys remnant assets like IP and recovery claims. Aldaron funded that deal with money from early investors, some of which also made direct investments in Oak Point. Aldaron continued raising money afterward, closing its first fund in October with $884 million from outside investors and more than $950 million in total including the coinvestments, Mendez said. The broader fundraising squeeze comes amid a yearslong slump in sales and initial public offerings of private equity-backed companies, leaving many firms with holdings they picked up in the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. Private equity firms are sitting on nearly 4,600 U.S. companies they've owned for at least five years, according to an August PitchBook report, longer than the industry's typical three- to five-year holding period. That means less cash is returning to the pension funds, endowments and other investors, known as limited partners, leaving them with less money to commit to new funds. The biggest private equity firms often have an edge in competing for fresh capital thanks to their long track records, along with their sizable sales teams that allow them to reach various pools of capital including wealthy individual investors. Smaller fund managers, particularly those that are trying to raise their second or third funds after struggling to return money to investors, could be squeezed out entirely. "We expect many managers to exit the market, and we are already seeing this as fundraising becomes more challenging," said Mitchell Mansfield, a managing director at Kroll and global head of fund solutions, which advises fund managers on restructuring and winding down funds. To be sure, leaning into AI is just one way smaller private equity firms are finding ways to distinguish themselves. Some are narrowing their focus to a particular sector rather than competing with funds that invest across industries. They can also offer investors more attractive terms, such as opportunities to coinvest in deals, often with lower fees. Fund managers can also put more of their own money into investments. Broadwing Capital Management, for instance, started buying companies before completing its first institutional fundraising, betting that an existing portfolio would help win over investors. "It's a lot easier to talk about an investment with folks than about the theory of a new firm," said co-founder and managing partner Eliot Kerlin, who launched Broadwing after 15 years at middle-market private equity firm Insight Equity. Broadwing, which focuses on manufacturing, industrial services and distribution businesses, launched in 2022 and made its first three acquisitions using money from outside investors and some of the founders' own capital before hiring a placement agent to raise a larger fund. The firm structured its early investments so they could become part of a growing fund as Broadwing raised more money. The strategy paid off-Broadwing closed its $440 million inaugural fund this August, surpassing its fundraising goal by $90 million. By then it already owned six companies. Goldman Sachs Says CEOs Are 'Leaning In' on Strategic M&A Strategic megadeals are dominating the tech mergers and acquisitions landscape right now, Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs' global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information's WTF Summit on Tuesday. That will likely continue, Posnett said, and the bank has a robust pipeline of deal talks across the board. "They're talking about really big deals, industry consolidation. They're talking about M&A to bridge strategic gaps. They're talking about M&A to drive growth. They're talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape," she said. "CEOs are leaning in right now and they want to make big strategic bets," she said, noting that there's "a ton of" strategic activity in tech specifically. Posnett's comments came ahead of DoorDash's Thursday announcement of a $17 billion deal to buy Instacart. (The Information was first to report last week that Instacart was in sale talks.) items.title: 'Skeptical' Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: As Anthropic correctly pointed out in its initial public offering filing, business use of AI is in its infancy. Many other corporate executives say it will take some time for white-collar workers, especially those who aren't software engineers, to use the latest tools effectively. For example, White & Case, a large global law firm with more than 2,000 lawyers, is "having to hold back" its rollout of one of the newest legal assistants made by AI startup Legora because lawyers are hesitant about using so-called AI agents, said Isabel Parker, the law firm's chief innovation officer. A gradual rollout will ensure lawyers feel confident in using the new agent, which can handle more complex legal work than the AI agent from Legora that lawyers currently use for tasks such as analyzing and summarizing documents and generating ideas, she said. Unlike simpler chatbots, AI agents can take multiple actions on behalf of the user. Lawyers "are not the kind of people that easily lend themselves to using AI," she told The Information's Laura Mandaro during the WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women leaders in tech and finance. They're "skeptical, they're time-poor, they're risk averse, and they have a very strong conviction that their expertise is very artisanal...This technology comes along and it's a threat to everything they worked for." Legora, a fast-growing app privately valued at roughly $9 billion, aims to automate legal work such as reviewing contracts and drafting documents-the kind of paperwork that needs to be error-free. In an email, Parker said White & Case is investing "significant amounts" in AI tools and that 90% of the firm's staff uses Legora's products to some extent. In some cases, using the products can save them as much as 80% of the time it took to manually perform tasks, she said. Legora's vice president of engagement, Jillian Burnett, said at the same event that the rapid pace of AI development means that lawyers must constantly learn new tools, which can wear them out. "We're working with a very skeptical [lawyer] client base overall, a very busy client base. And when they're already having to sit through trainings, different tools...lawyers aren't necessarily going to want to give you more of their billable time to learn something new," Burnett told Mandaro at the event. She said Legora "didn't appreciate that fatigue enough" as a challenge to getting customers to use its tools. Legora has worked to address this by sending its staff to work with lawyers to show how the products can be "hyper-relevant" to their work. Despite that resistance, Legora seems to be doing all right, and recently said it crossed $200 million in annualized recurring revenue. That implies it generates more than $16 million per month in revenue. What is forcing change on White & Case lawyers is their clients. Parker said clients routinely ask the firm how it's using new technologies to speed up work and how it can pass that "value" or new efficiencies to the clients. Now that both White & Case and the in-house legal teams of its clients often use the same AI apps and tools, "there's nowhere to hide," she said. "One thing that cuts through any change fatigue in a lawyer is the client saying, 'I want this done. Show me how you've been using this [AI tool],'" she said. In some cases, though, firms may intentionally slow AI use among junior employees to make sure they learn basic skills. For example, Parker said her firm is considering "sacrificing some efficiency" from AI so its junior lawyers can learn to do their work manually before adopting agents that can automate more difficult tasks such as Legora's Agent Pro. "Most planes are flown by autopilot now...but you need to make sure that whoever's...in the cockpit does know how to fly a plane," she said.
